The Scottish Enlightenment. An intellectual movement that flourished in eighteenth-century Scotland, roughly between seventeen thirty and seventeen ninety, transforming Western thought with groundbreaking ideas in philosophy, economics, and natural science.

This remarkable ferment was centered in Edinburgh and Glasgow, which became hubs of coffee-house debate and university life. Scotland was recovering economically in the latter half of the century after the failed Jacobite Rising of seventeen forty-five, and that recovery fueled intellectual ambition.

David Hume emerged as one of the movement's towering figures, developing a radical empiricism and skepticism that questioned even the nature of causation and innatism. His ideas would influence Kant and reshape the entire trajectory of philosophy. Adam Smith, perhaps equally influential, wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments in seventeen fifty-nine and The Wealth of Nations in seventeen seventy-six, establishing the foundational economic and social thought that would reshape capitalism itself.

Beyond philosophy and economics, the movement sparked breakthroughs in natural science. James Watt, Joseph Black, and other natural philosophers made discoveries in engineering, chemistry, and physics that directly enabled the Industrial Revolution. The characteristic spirit was one of skepticism toward received authority, a deep emphasis on observation and experience, and a practical commitment to applying ideas to improve society. This became known as the Scottish Age of Reason, and it distinguished itself from the Continental Enlightenment through its pragmatism, its skepticism, and its focus on natural philosophy rather than pure reason. Scotland, geographically remote from the European centers of the movement, punched far above its weight in shaping Western civilization.
